intro: Today's material splits into two honest gaps: agent benchmarks and memory research show how far the underlying technology still has to go, while the banking items show regulators and a top-tier bank both concluding that the rulebook and the platform for agentic AI aren't settled yet.

cards.title: τ²-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment
cards.bite: When an AI agent is tested in a lab setting where it alone controls all the tools, it can look highly capable — but real customer service and telecom scenarios involve a customer who can also take actions mid-conversation. This paper finds that adding an active human on the other side of the interaction causes success rates to collapse, in one case from about 74% down to 34% for the same underlying model. The bottleneck isn't the AI's reasoning — it's coordinating with an unpredictable second party who's also acting.
cards.read_if: Read if you sell or evaluate conversational agents for support or telecom use cases; skip if your interest is model architecture, not deployment realism.
cards.key_takeaway: Agent performance drops sharply when moving from solo control to dual-control with an active user — the paper's own analysis shows "pass@1 for GPT-4.1 drops from approximately 74% (retail/airline) to 34% (Telecom)," isolating communication/coordination overhead as a bigger bottleneck than raw reasoning.

cards.title: Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents: Mechanisms, Evaluation, and Emerging Frontiers
cards.bite: This paper builds a shared vocabulary for what 'agent memory' actually means, separating it clearly from just having a bigger context window. It breaks memory into how long information is kept, where it's stored, and how the agent decides what to write, keep, or retrieve — then surveys five different technical approaches to doing that well. The core point: an agent's ability to remember and improve over time is a design choice with real engineering tradeoffs, not a side effect of using a more powerful model.
cards.read_if: Read if you need precise language to explain 'does it remember me' to a technical or skeptical buyer; skip if you just need the one-paragraph version, which is above.
cards.key_takeaway: The paper's own framing states that <cite index="34-5,34-6">it formalizes agent memory as a write--manage--read loop tightly coupled with perception and action, then introduces a three-dimensional taxonomy spanning temporal scope, representational substrate, and control policy, examining five mechanism families in depth: context-resident compression, retrieval-augmented stores, reflective self-improvement, hierarchical virtual context, and policy-learned management</cite> — meaning memory quality, not model swaps, is usually the real differentiator in production agent behavior.

cards.title: SR 26-2: Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management (supersedes SR 11-7)
cards.source: Federal Reserve Board of Governors (with OCC and FDIC)
cards.bite: US banking regulators just replaced their fifteen-year-old model risk rulebook with a more flexible, principles-based framework — but they explicitly excluded generative and agentic AI from it, calling those systems too new and fast-moving to regulate yet. That means banks deploying agentic AI today are doing so under improvised extensions of old guidance, not a finished rule, while a formal industry-wide review is still pending. For anyone selling into a bank's model risk or compliance function, this is the difference between 'here are the rules' and 'we're figuring out the rules as we go.'
cards.read_if: Read if you sell any AI or model-driven tool into a US bank's risk, compliance, or model validation team; skip if your buyer is purely on the business/product side.
cards.key_takeaway: SR 26-2 replaces SR 11-7's prescriptive rules with a principles-based, risk-tailored framework (most directly binding on banks over $30B in assets), but it carves generative AI and agentic AI models out of scope entirely as "novel and rapidly evolving," pending a still-unpublished interagency RFI — meaning banks are governing today's agentic deployments under ad hoc extensions of old principles, not a settled rule.

cards.title: Why Capital One built its multi-agent AI platform around open-weight models
cards.bite: Capital One's ML engineering leadership explains why they didn't buy an off-the-shelf agent platform: no vendor combination hit their targets for cost, latency, and quality at the same time. Instead they fine-tuned open-weight models themselves, built their own system for coordinating multiple agents, and layered in their own governance controls. Their edge came from owning that full stack, not from picking a better vendor.
cards.read_if: Read if you're pitching a foundation-model API or agent platform to a large bank with serious engineering resources; skip if your target buyer is a smaller institution without an in-house ML org.
cards.key_takeaway: Capital One's competitive edge came from combining fine-tuned open-weight models, a proprietary multi-agent orchestration harness, and built-in enterprise governance — not from adopting a vendor's off-the-shelf foundation model — because generic platforms couldn't hit their cost, latency, and quality bars simultaneously.

cards.title: EU AI Act's High-Risk Deadline: Deferred, Not Cancelled
cards.bite: A newly enacted EU regulation pushes the deadline for high-risk AI obligations — including credit scoring systems — from August 2026 to December 2027, giving banks sixteen extra months before those rules bite. But it's not a full reprieve: transparency requirements and obligations on general-purpose AI providers stay on the original timeline. Banks that read this as 'AI Act compliance can wait' are only half right.
cards.read_if: Read if you're selling AI or compliance tooling into EU banks and need to know how urgent the buyer's timeline actually is; skip if your business is US-only.
cards.key_takeaway: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (the Digital Omnibus), in force since July 27 2026, pushes Annex III high-risk AI obligations — including credit scoring — from August 2026 to December 2027, but Article 50 transparency duties and GPAI provider obligations remain on the original schedule, so banks can't treat this as a blanket reprieve.
